frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access by non-standard processes, SAM/NTDS.dit or registry hive dumps, use of credential-dumping tools (e.g., Mimikatz, procdump on lsass), suspicious access to DPAPI secrets or browser credential stores, or anomalous authentication with harvested credentials.

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Hands-on-keyboard intrusion on scranton.dmevals.local by pbeesly (readme.ps1/psversion.ps1 from SysinternalsSuite, discovery, persistence, screen capture, clipboard, sdelete anti-forensics) culminating in full-access LSASS handle and LSA registry reads.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF then 0x1FFFFF on scranton at 03:05:16 UTC, confirmed by 4656 with AccessMask 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff; nashua wsmprovhost 0x1f3fff handle is benign Get-Process -IncludeUserName.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No reg save of SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM, no hive-copy file creations, no 4663 access to SAM/SECURITY hives.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit file access, no ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow execution, no NTDS object access.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: Masquerading C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr read HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa on scranton and was then wiped with sdelete64; single query-value access, no secret export observed.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No SECURITY\Cache registry access, no 4656 on SECURITY objects, no mscache/dcc PowerShell.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync, DirectorySearcher, Get-ADReplAccount or replication-API activity in PowerShell or security logs.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the legitimate Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local: netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes traceFile=...etl' / 'trace stop' at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z and 03:19:24Z, parented by NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service, with the Microsoft NDIS Capture (NdisCap) service start type toggled demand->system->demand around it. No pcap/npcap/WinPcap/WinDivert driver loads, no capture-related PowerShell, no promiscuous-mode or inbound 5156 artifacts. The malicious activity present (PsExec64 with cleartext credentials to NASHUA, python.exe PyInstaller payload, sdelete64 wiping) is lateral movement/evasion, not sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input/credential capture tooling (screen capture + LSASS handle access with full rights from PowerShell/WinRM host) executed by pbeesly on SCRANTON and NASHUA.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger APIs in script blocks, no scancode-map/keyboard-filter registry tampering, no keylogger service installed.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture PowerShell loop using System.Windows.Forms/CopyFromScreen captured the interactive desktop every 300s on SCRANTON.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/wwwroot page creation, no web-shell or fake login page scripts, no object access to web roots.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe (SCRANTON) and wsmprovhost.exe (NASHUA) opened lsass.exe/winlogon.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and an UNKNOWN call-trace module, indicating in-memory credential API access.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4740/4771 events in windows.security; the only 4776 NTLM validation succeeded (Status 0x0). No authentication-failure or lockout telemetry indicating brute force.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No hydra/ncrack/medusa command lines and no failed logons. PowerShell 'Password' hits are certificate .pfx export and 7-Zip archive encryption on scranton.dmevals.local, not password guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No reg save/ntdsutil/vssadmin, no hashcat/john/Invoke-Mimikatz, no hive or NTDS dumps (only WER crash dumps). SAM 4663 accesses are by lsass.exe under SCRANTON$; the PowerShell LSASS handle open (0x1fffff) is memory credential dumping, not offline cracking.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: All 4648 explicit-credential logons are the single account pbeesly (scranton->NASHUA and PSEXESVC on nashua), with no failures or lockouts — lateral movement with one known credential, not spraying across many accounts.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No curl/wget/Invoke-WebRequest credential submission and no 4625 events; the only hardcoded credential use is a single WebDAV mapping for exfiltration, not stuffing of many credential pairs.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No smartcard/SCardSvr/VaultSvc/credential-provider activity in any dataset: security-wide search for smartcard/vault/credential/NGC object, service and process names returned 0 hits, and the windows.other scardsvr/vaultsvc service check returned 0 hits. The only notable LSASS access (PowerShell.exe 0x1fffff on scranton at 03:05:16) belongs to a certificate/credential collection toolkit (Get-PrivateKeys Export-PfxCertificate from readme.ps1), i.e. credential/certificate theft rather than MFA interception. Kerberos KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and pbeesly 4648/PSEXESVC logons are normal pre-auth and lateral credential use.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: The WebDAV/SMB and NTLM hits are explained without forced authentication: the WebDAV traffic to 192.168.0.4 is the exfil upload leg of Invoke-Exfil, which supplies explicit credentials (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!) via New-PSDrive rather than coercing NTLM; the single NtLmSsp type-3 logon (pbeesly from 172.18.39.2) and LsaSrv 6038 warning on scranton are ordinary NTLM fallback; all 139/445 outbound connections are from the System process to internal hosts. No .scf/.url/.searchConnector-ms lures or attacker-controlled SMB/WebDAV coercion targets were observed.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local an attacker-controlled hidden PowerShell session (PID 2976, spawned by control.exe, decoding a payload from monkey.png) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff, alongside offensive PowerShell tooling (Get-AttributesMask, Keystroke-Check, Invoke-Exfil), a LocalSystem 'javamtsup' service install, PsExec with plaintext credentials to NASHUA and sdelete cleanup. A PowerShell Remoting session (wsmprovhost.exe) also opened LSASS with 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local. Remaining LSASS access is attributable to OS/Azure components and is benign.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, SYSTEM) opened MicrosoftEdge.exe/EdgeCP/EdgeSH with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and an UNKNOWN-module call trace at 03:05:17Z, during a malicious pbeesly session (steganographic IEX loader, credential-file archive staging, sdelete64, Invoke-Discovery). Full-access browser handles enable in-memory cookie theft, but no cookie file was read/copied and no script block referencing cookies was found, so the theft itself is not proven.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credential material (plaintext domain password in PsExec command line, hardcoded pfx password, registry-stored payload) was used and re-used across SCRANTON and NASHUA.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: PsExec64.exe used with cleartext password Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by to reach NASHUA, and the NASHUA python.exe/PowerShell chain harvested *pass*/*psw*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn* files into a password-protected RAR.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: hostui.exe (runas) spawned PowerShell reading HKLM\SOFTWARE\Javasoft 'value Supplement' and piping it to Invoke-Expression.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No PSReadLine/ConsoleHost_history/.bash_history file creation, process command line or 4663 access was found in any dataset.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported every LocalMachine certificate to Downloads\<random>.pfx with hardcoded password 'saribas', followed by Invoke-BeachCleanup deleting the .pfx files.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No Groups.xml/cpassword/gpprefdecrypt activity in PowerShell, Sysmon or Security; zeek SMB only shows gpt.ini and GptTmpl.inf reads on sysvol with no GPP credential file access.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 03:05:16 UTC and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 UTC, both under user pbeesly, corroborated by Security 4656 handle requests with the same masks — LSASS memory credential theft.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No hits for browser credential files (Login Data, logins.json, key4.db, Cookies, Web Data) in sysmon, security or PowerShell telemetry; only a benign svchost INetCookies write.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No vault/cmdkey/credential API usage, no file writes to \Microsoft\Credentials or \Microsoft\Vault; only a routine Credential Guard configuration event.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass process, file or script activity found in any dataset.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe and winlogon.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff and an UNKNOWN call-trace module at 03:05:16-03:05:17, inside a hands-on session that also installed the javamtsup service and ran discovery/persistence/private-key theft functions.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Logon process names are normal (Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp), network logons are machine accounts plus pbeesly, and no 4739 or lsass/cryptdll script activity exists; no DC authentication modification seen.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password-filter DLL written to System32, no Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry change, and only legitimate NotificationController DLLs loaded.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739, no Reversible object access, no Set-ADUser/ADAccountControl command lines; the single script-block hit is a TimeSpan validation fragment.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: Event 4739 is absent from both windows.security and windows.other; no MFA policy change recorded.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory modifications and no adfs/azuread script content; 5058/5061 events are routine KSP key opens by pbeesly and NEWYORK$.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider registry/file/4657 activity; winlogon handles come from system processes, with the anomalous PowerShell/wsmprovhost full-access handles reported under T1556.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: Only AiTM-relevant signal is the Zeek shared-MAC anomaly (12:34:56:78:9a:bc answering for 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and 192.168.0.4 concurrently from 00:30Z on 2020-04-30); no Windows-side corroboration possible because the Zeek window does not overlap the Windows datasets.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: DNS/LLMNR lookups resolved normally to correct internal IPs, wpad returned NXDOMAIN, SMB 445/139 connections were RSTO/REJ with no relay authentication, and the only NTLM network logon (pbeesly from 172.18.39.2) was LogonType 10 RDP, not SMB relay.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: One MAC (12:34:56:78:9a:bc) is recorded as responder for four distinct IPs including the DC 10.0.0.4 and NASHUA 10.0.1.6, with three IPs answered in the same 5-minute buckets from 00:30Z; consistent with ARP cache poisoning, though the placeholder MAC and lack of ARP logs keep confidence medium.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP server/client configuration events (1341/1342/1020/1063) in windows.other; only 3 routine ipconfig.exe executions and a built-in xDNSServerAddress DSC scriptblock run by SYSTEM on newyork.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: No Kerberos ticket theft/forging was observed, but the credential-access precondition was met: attacker-launched hidden PowerShell (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF, i.e. LSASS memory was accessible for credential/ticket extraction. Ticket-specific artefacts are absent, so the family is only partially supported.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 4768/4769 events are normal pre-authenticated AES256 TGT/TGS for pbeesly and machine accounts with Status 0x0; no krbtgt/DCSync/mimikatz strings in PowerShell or windows.other, no forged-ticket logon anomalies.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service-ticket requests are routine machine-account TGS (SCRANTON$->NEWYORK$/WEC$, pbeesly->NASHUA$) with AES256 and Status 0x0; no silver/kerberoast/SPN tooling strings and no anomalous service-account network logons.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No bulk RC4 (0x17) 4769 requests for distinct SPNs; all 4769 use 0x12, and Zeek shows only 11 successful aes256 TGS requests from pbeesly. No kerberoasting tooling in script blocks.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: Every AS exchange shows KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED followed by a successful pre-authenticated AS-REP; all 4768 have PreAuthType 2. No AS-REP roasting tooling or messages found.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web-credential artefacts. The high-privilege LSASS handles (PowerShell.exe 0x1fffff on scranton, wsmprovhost.exe 0x1f3fff on nashua) indicate credential enumeration/harvesting, not token forgery; 4624 stacks are Kerberos/Negotiate dominated with a single NTLM network logon.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-related file event is a LocalService INetCookies write by svchost.exe on scranton; no user browser cookie/Login Data/Web Data access and no cookie-referencing script blocks.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for ADFS/SAML strings in windows.other and for token/saml file creations in sysmon; no SAML token forging evidence.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 6 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a 'Get-PrivateKeys' PowerShell function (staged as C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) that recursively exported every cert:\LocalMachine certificate with a private key to random .pfx files in Downloads using a hardcoded password; Sysmon confirmed creation of C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe PID 3876, followed minutes later by an 'Invoke-BeachCleanup' function deleting Downloads\*.pfx. A separate 4657 on nashua.dmevals.local modified a ROOT\Certificates 'Blob' value (suspicious, low confidence). No PKINIT/certificate-based Kerberos logons were observed.

findings.title: pbeesly's PowerShell opened LSASS with full access (0x1fffff / 0x1f3fff) on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 UTC, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly, DMEVALS domain) on scranton.dmevals.local opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and then 0x1FFFFF — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-class masks used for memory dumping, with an UNKNOWN call trace (unbacked code). The same access is recorded in the Security channel as 4656 on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe by powershell.exe as pbeesly with AccessMask 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff. This occurred inside a hands-on-keyboard intrusion session on scranton (readme.ps1 / psversion.ps1 loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Get-Clipboard, Keystroke-Check, sdelete64 wiping of a malicious .scr). No dump file was observed on disk, but the LSASS read handle with full access by a non-system PowerShell is consistent with in-memory credential theft.

On scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:53Z and 03:05:59Z, user pbeesly executed PowerShell script blocks defining 'Invoke-ScreenCapture', which starts a background job that every 300 seconds grabs the full virtual screen via [System.Windows.Forms.SystemInformation]::VirtualScreen and System.Drawing CopyFromScreen and saves it as a .bmp in the user's Downloads folder (script path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1). This is GUI input/screen capture of the interactive session, part of the same pbeesly toolset that also ran Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip password-protected archive of Downloads) and the remote Get-Process/UserName enumeration. No fake credential prompt (Get-Credential/PromptForCredential) was observed; the only consent.exe hits are the normal UAC consent process.

At 03:09:29Z on nashua.dmevals.local the same pattern appears from wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM host for the remote PowerShell session) against lsass.exe (PID 728) and winlogon.exe with 0x1f3fff, call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll. This is the direct follow-on to the attacker's remote PowerShell: at 03:09:23Z user pbeesly on SCRANTON ran 'Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA -ScriptBlock { Get-Process -IncludeUserName ... }', which executed on NASHUA at 03:09:28Z in PID 7720 — the same PID that then opened LSASS. Security 4663 corroborates a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe from powershell.exe as pbeesly on SCRANTON at 03:05:16Z. The remaining LSASS/winlogon accesses (0x1000/0x1400/0x1478 from smss/wininit/lsasrv/themeservice, CollectGuestLogs.exe and MsMpEng.exe with 0x10) are normal system/AV behaviour.

That same PID 2976 then opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16.623Z and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16.654Z — full-process access masks consistent with reading LSASS memory for credential extraction. In the same session pbeesly loaded offensive PowerShell functions from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 / readme.ps1: Get-AttributesMask (token/group attribute parsing), Keystroke-Check (AV product enumeration), Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip staging to C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\OfficeSupplies.7z and WebDAV upload to \\192.168.0.4\webdav with hardcoded creds), and remote Invoke-Command to NASHUA. pbeesly also installed a LocalSystem service 'javamtsup' pointing at C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe (4697, 03:04:15Z) after dropping javamtsup.exe from the SysinternalsSuite archive, and used PsExec64 with plaintext credentials (dmevals\pbeesly / Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to run C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on NASHUA (PSEXESVC installed 4x). Sdelete64 was used to wipe staging artifacts. The LSASS access is not attributable to a signed security product or OS component; it comes from an interactive attacker-controlled PowerShell session, so it is assessed as exploitation/abuse for credential access rather than benign behaviour.

accesschk.exe writes a 'passwordsDB' file in SysinternalsSuite; harvested credentials reused via PsExec -p to NASHUA
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, accesschk.exe (parent powershell.exe, user pbeesly) was launched at 2020-05-02T03:04:34Z and created C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB at 03:04:35Z — a file name indicating collected credentials, written into the same SysinternalsSuite directory that hosted the attacker's readme.ps1/psversion.ps1 scripts. Minutes later (03:11:18–03:14:42Z) PsExec64.exe was run four times from the same directory with an explicit plaintext credential: \\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, and nashua.dmevals.local logged 4648 explicit-credential logons from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe for pbeesly. findings.summary: Across the Windows datasets (2020-05-02) there is no evidence of traffic interception: outbound Sysmon 3 destinations are the normal internal peers (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.4, 10.0.1.6, 192.168.0.4) plus Microsoft/Internet ranges, and object-access events (4663/4656/4670) are dominated by routine registry reads (Session Manager\Environment, Lsa, Winlogon). The only AiTM-relevant anomaly is the Zeek MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answering for 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and 192.168.0.4 concurrently from 00:30Z on 2020-04-30, which is reported under T1557.002. findings.title: Single MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answering for three distinct IPs (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, 192.168.0.4) in Zeek conn logs
findings.summary: In the Zeek window (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45Z) the responding L2 address 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is recorded for four different destination IPs: 10.0.0.4 (120 conns, 00:06:38-00:43:59), 10.0.1.6 (44 conns, 00:33:26-00:45:00), 192.168.0.4 (392 conns, 00:32:14-00:44:44) and 192.168.0.5 (3 conns, 00:08:02-00:15:18). From 00:30Z onward the same MAC answers for three IPs within the same 5-minute buckets (42, 66 and 404 conns), which is the classic signature of one device claiming multiple IPs on the segment (ARP cache poisoning / on-path interception). Notably 10.0.0.4 is the domain controller NEWYORK (DNS answers for newyork.dmevals.local resolve to 10.0.0.4) and 10.0.1.6 is NASHUA, so traffic to the DC and to a member server appears to be answered by the same MAC. Caveat: 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a well-known placeholder MAC and the Zeek sensor may be normalising/rewriting MACs, so this could be a capture artefact rather than real poisoning; no ARP-specific log source is available to confirm. No Windows-side corroboration exists because the Windows datasets (2020-05-02) do not overlap the Zeek window (2020-04-30).

findings.title: No forged web-credential material observed; LSASS access on scranton/nashua is PowerShell/.NET credential-enumeration tooling, not token forgery
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 the only high-privilege LSASS handles in the window came from PowerShell-based tooling, not from any web-credential forging utility. At 03:05:16 on scranton.dmevals.local PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and then 0x1fffff with a CallTrace ending in UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D) — an unbacked/private code region, i.e. in-memory .NET/PowerShell code rather than a signed DLL. At 03:09:29 on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, PowerShell Remoting host) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff, the call trace running through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll — consistent with PowerShell credential/privilege enumeration (e.g. token/group enumeration) executed over WinRM. Both are consistent with the credential-access hypothesis (harvesting), but nothing in the data shows creation or use of forged web credentials: no SAML/ADFS artefacts, no cookie-store theft, and the 4624 logon-process/authentication-package stacks are dominated by Kerberos (217) and Negotiate (78) with only a single NTLM/NtLmSsp logon (pbeesly, logon type 3, from 172.18.39.2 at 03:20:41 on scranton), which is a normal remote-auth pattern rather than forged-token use. The 4648 explicit-credential events are pbeesly re-authenticating to localhost via PSEXESVC on nashua and normal DWM-/UMFD-/machine-account logons on scranton.

On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02 03:16:19 UTC, Security event 4657 shows the registry value 'Blob' under \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 being modified, with the modifying process reported as C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe running as NASHUA$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3e7). This is the only 4657 touching a certificate store in the whole dataset (all other 4657s are WMI Autologger EventLog-Application keys written by wevtutil.exe). A change to a trusted root certificate blob is consistent with root CA store tampering, but the recorded process name is anomalous for a genuine certificate install (Sysmon does not manage certificate stores) and the old/new values are not auditable for REG_BINARY, so the actual content change cannot be verified. No matching certificate export, PKINIT logon or forged-certificate use was observed on nashua, so this is recorded as suspicious rather than confirmed malicious.

findings.title: No hybrid-identity (AD FS / Azure AD / federation) tampering observed
findings.summary: No 5136 directory-object modification events exist in windows.security or windows.other, and no PowerShell script block references adfs/azuread/federation-related terms. The 5058/5061 events present are routine KSP key operations: on scranton pbeesly opened machine RSA key {ADA1F326-B4FE-4C0C-B68C-1B4CA6F364AC} via 'Microsoft Software Key Storage Provider' (Operation 'Open Key', ReturnCode 0x0) at 2020-05-01T23:04:57-04:00, and NEWYORK$ performed similar key operations - consistent with the Get-PrivateKeys certificate activity, not with federation trust modification.

incidents.title: Hidden PowerShell (PID 2976) opens LSASS and winlogon with full-access masks on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: All describe the same event: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 as pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe (and winlogon.exe) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and an UNKNOWN call trace, plus the wsmprovhost.exe LSASS access on NASHUA from the same operator. Full-access handles to LSASS memory are the defining behavior of OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory (T1003.001); the findings' alternate labels (T1056.004, T1212, T1555, T1556, T1558, T1606) describe the same observed action, which is best fit by T1003.001.

incidents.title: Masqueraded .scr loader in C:\ProgramData\victim reads LSA registry key and drops steganographic carrier on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: The cod.3aka3.scr loader (launched from explorer.exe, later wiped with sdelete) read HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa, which holds LSA secrets, and dropped monkey.png; sdclt.exe/control.exe UAC-bypass activity is part of the same loader chain. The credential-relevant action is reading the Lsa key, best fit by LSA Secrets (T1003.004); the loader/UAC-bypass steps are the surrounding execution chain.

incidents.title: PowerShell screen-capture loop run by pbeesly on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: Invoke-ScreenCapture periodically grabs the full virtual screen via CopyFromScreen and saves .bmp files — GUI input/screen capture, best fit by GUI Input Capture (T1056.002).

incidents.title: wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell Remoting session) opens LSASS with 0x1F3FFF on NASHUA
incidents.rationale: not grouped by the consolidation step

incidents.title: PowerShell opens Microsoft Edge processes with full access on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: PowerShell PID 2976 opened MicrosoftEdge.exe/MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe/MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe with 0x1FFFFF and an UNKNOWN call trace; full-access handles to a browser process are the prerequisite for reading session cookies, best fit by Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539).

incidents.title: accesschk.exe writes passwordsDB and harvested credentials reused via PsExec -p to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: accesschk.exe created C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB and PsExec64.exe was then run with the cleartext credential '-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by' against NASHUA. The credential-access action is credentials collected into a file, best fit by Credentials In Files (T1552.001); the PsExec use is the subsequent lateral movement.

incidents.title: Registry value HKLM\SOFTWARE\Javasoft 'value Supplement' used as hidden payload store and re-executed via Invoke-Expression
incidents.rationale: PowerShell set the registry value to a base64 hidden PowerShell command and later retrieved it with Get-ItemPropertyValue | Invoke-Expression, including a re-execution via hostui.exe runas. Credentials/payload stored and read from the registry is best fit by Credentials in Registry (T1552.002).

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: Same script block (readme.ps1, Get-PrivateKeys) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and calling Export-PfxCertificate into Downloads with hardcoded password 'saribas', followed by Invoke-BeachCleanup deleting the .pfx files. Exporting private-key certificates is best fit by Private Keys (T1552.004).

incidents.title: Shared MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answering for multiple IPs in Zeek logs
incidents.rationale: One L2 address answering for 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and 192.168.0.4 concurrently is the signature of ARP cache poisoning; F43 confirms no end-to-end AiTM chain beyond this anomaly. Best fit is ARP Cache Poisoning (T1557.002).

incidents.title: Root certificate store 'Blob' value modified on NASHUA
incidents.rationale: Security 4657 shows the ROOT\Certificates\BE36A456... 'Blob' value modified on nashua.dmevals.local — the only certificate-store modification in the dataset. Tampering with the certificate store is best fit by Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates (T1649).

incidents.title: Hidden PowerShell compiles attacker C# with csc.exe into DLLs on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: csc.exe compiling attacker C# into qkbkqqbs.dll and 0piklvia.dll from the hidden PowerShell is tooling execution, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information) for the in-memory/compiled payload staging.

incidents.title: PyInstaller python.exe pushed via PsExec to NASHUA beacons to 192.168.0.4:8443 and archives credential-named files
incidents.rationale: python.exe launched by PSEXESVC as pbeesly opened 348 outbound connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 and spawned PowerShell that enumerated the profile for credential-named files and packed them into a password-protected RAR. The observed action is collection/exfiltration staging and C2, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2 Channel).
